guide.title: Equal exposure is not equal image. Decide which cost you are willing to pay before you touch a dial.
guide.summary: Shutter speed, aperture and ISO each admit or amplify light, and each one changes something else while doing it: motion rendering, depth of field, or noise. Because a stop of one can be traded for a stop of another, it is easy to treat them as interchangeable. They are not — two frames with identical brightness can differ completely in what is sharp, what is blurred and how clean the shadows are.
points: A stop is a doubling or halving of light, and every control moves in the same unit — that is what makes them tradeable at all.
Shutter speed decides how motion is rendered: frozen, smeared, or somewhere in between. This is a subject decision before it is an exposure decision.
Aperture decides how much of the scene is acceptably sharp, and at the extremes it also costs resolution — wide open to aberrations, stopped far down to diffraction.
ISO does not collect light. It amplifies what the sensor already captured, so it raises the visibility of noise rather than creating it.
The meter assumes an average scene reflects mid-grey. Snow and black cats both break that assumption, in opposite directions.
